context.text: The Fourth Crusade set out for Egypt and never arrived. Debt to Venice diverted it first to the Christian city of Zara, then, entangled in a Byzantine succession dispute and unpaid promises, to Constantinople itself.

narrative.text: On April 12–13, 1204, the crusaders breached the sea walls and took the greatest city in Christendom. The three-day sack that followed appalled even its chroniclers: palaces and churches plundered, the altar and sanctuary of Hagia Sophia stripped and desecrated, relics carried off wholesale to the West, where many remain. 'Even the Saracens are merciful compared with these men who bear the Cross of Christ on their shoulders,' wrote the Byzantine senator and eyewitness Nicetas Choniates.

A Latin emperor was crowned in Hagia Sophia and a Venetian set up as patriarch; Orthodox bishops were displaced across the conquered lands. The Byzantine government-in-exile at Nicaea kept the Orthodox patriarchate alive until Michael VIII Palaiologos retook the City in 1261, but the empire never recovered its strength, and the East never forgot.

significance.text: More than 1054's anathemas, 1204 made the schism a fact in the Orthodox heart: the difference between estranged brothers and enemies. Every later reunion attempt negotiated in its shadow. In 2001 Pope John Paul II formally expressed sorrow for the sack; the wound remains part of Orthodox memory.
